clinicalPearls: Causes recurrent episodes of flaccid weakness that are typically shorter and more frequent than in the hypokalaemic form, often beginning in early childhood
Attacks are provoked by rest after exercise, fasting, cold exposure and ingestion of potassium-rich foods
Serum potassium rises or stays in the upper normal range during an attack because potassium moves out of muscle, though it may be normal by the time it is measured
Inherited as an autosomal dominant trait caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SCN4A skeletal-muscle sodium channel gene
Clinical or electrical myotonia, particularly of the eyelids, frequently coexists and helps distinguish it from the hypokalaemic form
Ingesting carbohydrate or gentle continued activity can abort an evolving attack, and prophylaxis uses carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or potassium-lowering measures such as thiazide diuretics
Allelic overlap with paramyotonia congenita and the potassium-aggravated myotonias means phenotypes can blend within families
reference.pathophysiology: Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis is caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A, the gene for the alpha subunit of the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.4. The mutant channels fail to inactivate completely, producing a persistent inward sodium current that keeps the sarcolemma partially depolarised. A modest rise in extracellular potassium further depolarises the membrane, and when depolarisation is sufficient the sodium channels become inactivated and the fibre inexcitable, causing flaccid paralysis. When depolarisation is milder it instead produces repetitive firing experienced as myotonia, explaining the frequent overlap of weakness and stiffness in affected individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary hyperkalaemia from renal failure, adrenal insufficiency or medication
Acute neuromuscular weakness such as Guillain-Barre syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium and electrocardiogram during a spontaneous attack
Electromyography to detect myotonic discharges between or during attacks
Short and prolonged exercise electromyography protocols demonstrating characteristic compound muscle action potential changes
Renal and adrenal assessment to exclude secondary causes of hyperkalaemia
Muscle biopsy where a fixed myopathy or diagnostic uncertainty exists
redFlags: Respiratory compromise or unusually prolonged, severe weakness during an attack
Cardiac arrhythmia associated with rising potassium
Hyperkalaemia due to a coexisting renal or endocrine disorder requiring separate treatment
Development of a fixed proximal myopathy with permanent weakness
reference.prognosis: Attacks tend to be brief and frequent in childhood and often become milder in adult life, and most patients have a normal life expectancy, although some develop a slowly progressive fixed proximal myopathy over time.
pitfalls: Measuring potassium too late, when a transiently elevated level has already returned to normal
Failing to recognise coexisting myotonia that would point away from the hypokalaemic form
Attributing hyperkalaemia to primary renal or adrenal disease and missing the channelopathy
Overlooking that potassium supplementation or potassium-rich diets can precipitate rather than relieve attacks
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Terminate early attacks with carbohydrate ingestion or mild sustained activity, and consider an inhaled beta-agonist to shift potassium intracellularly
Prevent recurrent attacks with a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor such as acetazolamide or with a thiazide diuretic to lower potassium
Counsel on avoiding provoking factors including fasting, cold exposure, potassium-rich foods and rest after exertion
Encourage a potassium-sparing, carbohydrate-rich dietary pattern with regular meals
Manage coexisting myotonia where symptomatic, for example with a sodium-channel-blocking agent
Monitor serum potassium and the electrocardiogram during attacks and watch for a progressive fixed proximal myopathy
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and manage through a neuromuscular service
